title: Mars surface imagery — how the layers work
intro_sentence: Zoom from the whole planet down to a rover's wheel tracks and you are looking at six layers of imagery from orbiters and rovers, stacked on top of each other and swapped in as you get closer.
seo_title: Mars Surface Imagery: How the Map Layers Work |||
seo_description: Mars Surface Imagery: How the Map Layers Work |||
narrative_101: No single camera can show you both the whole of Mars and a rover. A view of the full globe resolves several kilometres per pixel; the sharpest camera in orbit resolves a quarter of a metre but sees a strip only a few kilometres wide. So the map keeps several layers, each sharper and smaller than the one below, and shows whichever one fits the view, the same idea online maps use on Earth.

Think of it as a stack of slices hovering one above the other. The bottom slice is one image of the whole planet. Each slice above covers less ground in more detail. At the very top you are standing on the surface, looking through the rover's own cameras.

Every slice is the work of a different mission, and together they span more than fifty years. [Mariner 9](app:/missions?id=mariner9) became the first spacecraft to orbit another planet in 1971 and mapped Mars from orbit: it photographed about 85% of the surface. The two Viking orbiters, starting with [Viking 1](app:/fleet?id=viking1-orbiter) in 1976, photographed the whole planet, the basis of the first global mosaics. Today Europe's [Mars Express](app:/missions?id=mars-express), China's [Tianwen-1](app:/missions?id=tianwen1) and NASA's [Mars Odyssey](app:/fleet?id=mars-odyssey) and [Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter](app:/fleet?id=mro) keep photographing it; the last two supply most of the layers here.
body_paragraphs: Level 0 is the globe: a 4096-pixel global texture wrapped around the sphere. Mars's equator is about 21,300 km long, so each pixel spans roughly 5 km — enough for the volcanoes, canyons and polar caps, not for a single landing site. Level 1 is the context layer: around the site you have selected, a 400 km piece of the daytime infrared mosaic made by THEMIS, the Thermal Emission Imaging System on Mars Odyssey, is draped over the planet at its true latitude and longitude, about 100 m per pixel. THEMIS sees heat, not light: by day, slopes facing the Sun are warmer than slopes facing away, so the infrared mosaic reads largely like a shaded relief map of every crater rim and channel. It has no colour of its own, so the layer takes its colour and brightness from the globe and only its sharp detail from THEMIS, and it fades softly into the globe at the edges.

Level 2 is the regional view, about 15 km of ground around the landing point, from the Context Camera (CTX) on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. CTX is a pushbroom camera: one line of pixels sweeps across the ground as the orbiter moves, building a strip about 30 km wide at about 6 m per pixel. Since 2006 those strips have covered almost the entire planet, and Caltech's Murray Lab stitched them into the global mosaic this layer is cut from. Level 3 is the detail view: 512 m around the lander from HiRISE, the telescope camera on the same orbiter, whose half-metre mirror resolves 0.25 to 0.3 m per pixel. Both cameras fly in a [sun-synchronous orbit](orbits/sun-synchronous), passing over each place at the same local time of day, so pictures taken years apart share the same lighting.

Level 4 is the route tiles. Along the drives of [Spirit](app:/fleet?id=spirit), [Opportunity](app:/fleet?id=opportunity), [Curiosity](app:/fleet?id=curiosity) and [Perseverance](app:/fleet?id=perseverance), HiRISE images are cut into 512 m tiles at the notable stops, and for Curiosity and Perseverance at every half kilometre of the drive as well, so the whole route can be followed at close range. HiRISE is sharp enough to show landers, parachutes and heat shields; in 2012 it even photographed Curiosity hanging under its parachute on the way down. Level 5 is the panorama: the view from the ground, stitched from the rovers' and landers' own cameras, from Spirit and Opportunity's Pancam to Curiosity's Mastcam, Perseverance's Mastcam-Z, the [Phoenix](app:/fleet?id=phoenix) lander's stereo camera and China's [Zhurong](app:/fleet?id=zhurong).

How the layers meet. Each layer sits a hair above the one below, so the sharper image always wins where both exist, and each fades in by camera distance rather than popping in. At middle zooms the regional, detail and route patches are drawn larger than their true size so that you can see them at all; the imagery card says so. Zoom in further and the view switches to a flat patch at true scale. The imagery card in the corner always names the camera, the resolution and the licence of every layer on screen, and links to the source.

How the pictures reach you. The original crops are kept untouched in the project's archive. What your browser downloads are copies in several sizes, from 512 to 4096 pixels wide, and your device's quality setting picks the size: a phone on a slow connection gets the small one, a desktop on the cinematic setting the largest. The Moon is mapped the same way, by other spacecraft: see [Moon surface imagery](planets/moon-surface-imagery).
diagram_caption: Mars's six layers of imagery, from the whole-globe texture at the base to the rovers' own panoramas at the top, with the camera, resolution and ground covered by each.
